questions.q: In synchronous commit mode, when does the primary report a transaction as successfully committed to the client?
options: Synchronous commit never reports success back to the client
Only after all secondaries in every AG on the server confirm
Only after the secondary confirms it has hardened (durably logged) the corresponding log record
Immediately, without waiting for the secondary at all
questions.explain: Synchronous commit means the primary waits for the secondary's hardening confirmation before telling the client the write succeeded — this is what guarantees zero data loss.

questions.q: What is the main cost of synchronous commit, per this lesson?
options: It disables read-only queries on all secondaries
Permanent data loss on every failover
It requires SIMPLE recovery model
Added write latency, since the primary waits on the secondary's confirmation — which is why synchronous replicas are kept close together on low-latency networks
questions.explain: Waiting for the secondary's hardening confirmation adds latency proportional to network round-trip time, which is why sync replicas are typically kept nearby.

questions.q: What is the risk of asynchronous commit mode, per this lesson?
options: Asynchronous commit disables the transaction log entirely
If the primary fails before the secondary hardens the most recent log records, those transactions are lost on failover to that secondary
Every write is permanently rejected until the secondary confirms
There is no risk — asynchronous commit guarantees zero data loss just like synchronous
questions.explain: Because the primary doesn't wait for the secondary, any log records not yet hardened on the secondary at the moment of primary failure are lost.

questions.q: Why does SQL Server require synchronous commit mode for automatic failover, per this lesson?
options: Because automatically promoting an asynchronous secondary could silently lose data with no human confirming that's acceptable
Because automatic failover is only a licensing restriction, unrelated to data safety
It doesn't — automatic failover works fine with asynchronous commit
Because asynchronous commit is technically incompatible with having a listener
questions.explain: SQL Server enforces this pairing because automatic failover to an out-of-sync asynchronous replica could lose data without any human review — asynchronous replicas can only be failed over to manually.

questions.q: A secondary replica 2,000 miles away is configured for synchronous commit, hoping for zero data loss. What real problem does this cause, per this lesson?
options: It causes no problems at all — distance never matters for synchronous commit
This configuration is impossible and SQL Server would reject it outright
Every write on the primary now waits on the long cross-country network round trip, adding significant latency to normal application performance
It automatically converts the replica to asynchronous commit behind the scenes
questions.explain: Synchronous commit forces every write to wait for the distant secondary's confirmation, so long-distance replicas should generally use asynchronous commit instead to avoid crippling write latency.
